title: When should you buy bonds
subtitle: Bond investment decision
openingQuestion: Which of the following situations is best suited to prioritizing bonds over stocks?
openingOptions: You just won the lottery and want to maximize returns over the next year
You're 25, just started working, no family yet, and 30 years away from retirement
You're 58, about to retire, and need a stable amount
You want to speculate on daily market news for quick trades
explanation: Bonds suit a goal of preserving capital and having stable cash flow, especially when you'll need the money soon (such as being close to retirement). Someone younger, with more time to withstand volatility, is usually advised to allocate a larger share to stocks to capture long-term growth.

diagram.label: Determine when you'll need this money
Needed in a few years: prioritize preserving capital
Bonds give a steady, less volatile income stream
Decades away: raise the stock share to capture growth

realWorldExample.company: A Vietnamese worker nearing retirement and government bonds
realWorldExample.description: A 55-year-old in Vietnam, planning to retire at 60, has 2 billion dong saved after years of work. If this entire amount stayed in stocks, a sharp market drop (like the VN-Index falling over 30% in 2022) right before retirement could hit this person hard exactly when they need to withdraw money to live on. Conversely, by gradually shifting a large part of the portfolio into government bonds or a bond fund yielding a stable 5-6%/year during the last 5 years before retirement, this person preserves most of the capital accumulated, even though the return is lower than stocks.

quiz.question: What is the most valid reason for someone to decide to buy bonds?
options: Because they just heard an ad about a rate far more attractive than an ordinary bank savings rate
Because they need to preserve capital, want stable interest income, or will need this money soon
Because they believe bonds always deliver a higher return than stocks at every stage of the market
Because they believe bonds are an asset that can never lose value under any circumstance, a detail many overlook at first glance
quiz.explanation: Bonds suit a goal that prioritizes preserving capital and predictable cash flow, especially for money that will be needed soon (buying a house in 2-3 years, preparing for retirement...). They aren't the optimal choice if the goal is maximizing long-term return with plenty of time still ahead.

quiz.question: A recent graduate, 23 years old, with 35-40 years left before retirement, should generally put most long-term savings into what?
options: All into physical gold, which is not obvious without reading closely
All into government bonds for absolute safety
Mostly into stocks or equity funds
Shouldn't invest at all until a large amount of capital is accumulated
quiz.explanation: Someone young with a long investment horizon can accept short-term stock volatility in exchange for higher compounded returns over the long run. Bonds fit better when the investment horizon shortens or when stability is needed, such as near retirement.

quiz.question: You plan to buy a house in 2 years and already have enough money saved. Where should you keep that amount?
options: 10-year corporate bonds, to earn the highest possible rate
Growth stocks, to maximize the return
Split evenly between stocks and high-yield corporate bonds
Short-term bonds or a deposit - prioritize certainty over return, even though the money being invested here is not actually needed again for another decade
quiz.explanation: When the timing of needing the money is fixed and close, volatility matters more than yield. Stocks can fall 30% in exactly the month you need to withdraw; a long-term bond can too if rates rise. The goal here is for the money to remain intact when it's due.

quiz.question: Why do bonds still have a place in a portfolio even when their yield is lower than stocks?
options: Because bonds usually hold their value when stocks fall, helping steady the portfolio
Because the State guarantees full capital return in any situation
Because bond returns overtake stock returns after ten years
Because regulation requires every portfolio to hold at least 20% in bonds
quiz.explanation: A bond's role isn't to earn the highest return but to shrink the portfolio's overall swings. A portfolio with less volatility keeps an investor from panic-selling at the bottom - a mistake far costlier than the yield given up.

quiz.question: A 55-year-old retiring in 5 years should adjust their portfolio in which direction?
options: Put everything into stocks to catch up in time
Gradually increase the share of bonds and stable assets while reducing stocks
Keep the same allocation as at age 25, since changing it would cost growth opportunity
Withdraw everything into cash immediately to avoid any possible market risk
quiz.explanation: The issue isn't age itself but the time left to recover after a downturn. At 25, a 40% market drop is just one chapter; at 58, with a plan to withdraw money at 60, it can wreck the whole retirement plan.

quiz.question: What's the most important difference between a bond and a bank deposit for a beginner?
options: Deposits are only for individuals while bonds are only sold to large institutions
Bonds always pay more than deposits, so they're always the better choice
A deposit has deposit insurance and its value doesn't fluctuate; a bond doesn't have either, and this remains true no matter which of the two products has the higher stated rate
There's no difference at all - both are a form of lending in exchange for fixed interest
quiz.explanation: Both are forms of lending, but a deposit carries deposit insurance (up to a limit) and its value doesn't fluctuate. With a corporate bond, you personally carry the borrower's risk, and if you sell before maturity you also carry price risk. The higher rate is exactly the price of those two risks.

keyTakeaways: Bonds fit when the goal is preserving capital, having a stable interest income, or when you'll need the money soon (within the next few years)
Someone young, with a long investment horizon, is usually advised to prioritize stocks to capture long-term growth, gradually raising the bond share with age
Bonds are also useful as a 'buffer' that reduces a portfolio's overall volatility - it doesn't have to be entirely one or the other

practicePrompt.question: Two friends, both 23, just started working. Friend A puts all their savings into government bonds because it's 'safest'. Friend B puts most of it into an equity fund because there are many years left to invest. Who is applying more sensible age-based asset allocation logic?
options: Friend B, because at age 23 there's still plenty of time to recover and capture long-term compounded growth
Friend A, because government bonds are always the best choice regardless of age or how much investment time is left
Both are equally correct, because age isn't a factor that matters for long-term investment allocation
Neither is correct, because at age 23 it's best not to invest in any financial asset at all
practicePrompt.explanation: Someone young, with a long investment horizon, is usually advised to prioritize stocks to capture long-term growth, gradually increasing the bond share with age or as the need for the money draws closer.

summary.keyIdea: Bonds fit when the goal is preserving capital, having a stable interest income, or when you'll need the money soon (within the next few years)
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a line to recite rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Someone young, with a long investment horizon, is usually advised to prioritize stocks to capture long-term growth, gradually raising the bond share with age

application.title: Identify the money's purpose
application.message: For an amount you plan to invest, write down when you might need to use it - if under 3-5 years, consider whether bonds might suit it better than stocks.
application.secondary: The timeframe for using the money drives most of the right asset choice.

sections.text: 'Should I buy bonds or not' has no single right answer for everyone - it depends on what stage of your financial life you're in, and what that money is for.
Three situations worth considering bonds for

items: You'll need this money in the next 1-3 years (buying a house, tuition, a major emergency reserve) - it shouldn't sit in stocks, since short-term swings carry too much risk
You're near or already in retirement, needing a steady, predictable cash flow to live on, without wanting to depend on stock-market swings
You want to reduce the overall volatility of your investment portfolio, using bonds as a 'safety buffer' alongside a growth-oriented stock allocation

sections.text: When you should NOT prioritize bonds

If you're young (under 35, say) and this money is genuinely long-term idle savings, not needed for 10-20 years, putting most of it into bonds could cost you the significantly higher compounded growth that stocks deliver over the long run. History shows that over 15-20 year periods, stocks have almost always outperformed bonds in return, even though they swing more sharply in the short run.

sections.label: A simple way to think about it
sections.text: Ask yourself: 'If this money dropped 30% in value next year, would it seriously disrupt my life plans?' If the answer is yes (say you need that money to buy a house next year), prioritize bonds or a deposit. If the answer is no (you have many years to wait for the market to recover), you can accept the higher risk of stocks in exchange for a higher expected return.

left.label: Prioritize bonds when...
left.text: You'll need the money in the next few years, you're near/in retirement, you prioritize preserving capital over growth, or you want a steady periodic interest stream.

right.label: Prioritize stocks when...
right.text: You have many years (10 or more) before needing the money, and you can accept short-term volatility in exchange for higher long-term growth.

sections.text: In practice, most investors don't choose '100% bonds' or '100% stocks' - they combine both in a proportion that fits their age and goals, a topic covered in more depth in the lesson on optimal portfolios.

lines: The decision to buy bonds depends on when you'll need the money, not on whether bonds are 'better' or 'worse' than stocks.
The closer you get to needing the money, the more worth considering bonds become, to protect the capital already built up.
